gap: No result ChatGPT got says how fast a no-solar battery refills once the grid is down. An Anker SOLIX E10 with two batteries holds 12.288 kWh. That runs an average US home (29.6 kWh/day) for about 10 hours. Anker's 4,500 W Smart Generator 5500 refills it in about 2.7 hours. A 240 V portable generator charges it at only about 20 A (4,800 W) until the owner enters the generator's running wattage in the app; the 240 V input itself goes up to 7,680 W.
standout_why: I read the cited West Electric comparison (westelectric.energy/batteries/compare-batteries). It gives only capacity (Powerwall 3 13.5 kWh, IQ 5P 5.0 kWh, aPower 2 15 kWh). It says that without solar a battery 'can only ride out a single outage cycle', and it mentions FranklinWH's 'native generator integration' with no charging rate. ChatGPT's own answer gives runtime (27 kWh / 20 kWh/day = 1.2 days) but no refill rate, no generator size and no input limit. I could not read three rivals: Tesla's How Powerwall Works page returned HTTP 403, and the FranklinWH user manual PDF came back as image-only. So I can't rule out that those two state a generator charging rate, which is why the score is 2, not 3. None of the pages I could read covers the refill numbers or the app setting that caps generator charging.
kit_items: Battery + inverter: Anker SOLIX E10 Power Module + 2× B6000 (12.288 kWh, 7,680 W continuous, 120/240 V split phase). Two batteries cover about 10 h of an average US home (29.6 kWh/day). One module takes up to 5 batteries (30.72 kWh, about 25 h). Its 240 V AC input recharges at 7,680 W, so it refills from the grid in about 1.6 h.

Transfer switch / panel: Anker SOLIX Power Dock (200 A service entry, ≤20 ms switchover, 12-circuit load management). It is needed because the E10's 7,680 W continuous output (32 A at 240 V) is far below what a 200 A house can draw. The dock's circuit management keeps the load under that limit.

Refill source (the replacement for solar): Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 (Tri-Fuel), 4,500 W DC into the E10 on gasoline or LPG and 4,000 W on natural gas. It refills 12.288 kWh in about 2.7 h. A 2.64 gal tank gives about 17 kWh, so an average 29.6 kWh/day home uses about 1.74 tanks (about 4.6 gal) a day.

Alternative refill: a 240 V portable generator you already own, connected to the E10's AC input. Set its running wattage under AC Input Settings → 240 V Portable Generator. Otherwise EV Outdoors saw charging held at about 20 A (4,800 W). A 120 V generator charges at only 1,800 W, and Anker says continuous charging above 12 A should stay under 3 hours, so plan on 1,440 W, which is about 8.5 h for 12.288 kWh.
